subtype: Hiraeth for a home and language left behind [Actor]

"You're humming again," Hansa said, looking up from her laptop.
Deepika stopped. "Was I? It's a Garhwali song. My Nani sang it while she shelled peas."
"Sing it properly then."
"I can't. Half the words are gone." Deepika pulled her knees up on the hostel bed. "Nobody here says anything the way we say it at home. I told the canteen man the dal was 'khatu' and he stared at me."
"So you miss the language."
"The language, the lanes going uphill, the Diwali lamps on every step. Even the smell of wet pine after rain." She laughed a little. "Though honestly, our lanes were muddy, the power went off every evening, and I spent every festival arguing with my cousins."
"And you'd still go back tomorrow?"
"Tomorrow. Tonight, if the bus left now."
Hansa closed the laptop. "Then teach me one word a day. Start with khatu."

qa.q: Who used to sing the Garhwali song while shelling peas?
qa.a: Deepika's Nani sang it while she shelled peas.

qa.q: What is Deepika feeling when she says she would go back tonight if the bus left now?
qa.a: She is homesick and aching for home, even while she admits the lanes were muddy and the power went off; her longing makes home feel better than it really was.

qa.q: What small step could help Deepika carry her home with her in this city?
qa.a: She could take up Hansa's offer and teach her a word a day, or find other Garhwali speakers, so her language stays alive in her everyday life here.

qa.q: How does Hansa seem to see Deepika's homesickness?
qa.a: Hansa takes it seriously and kindly; instead of telling her to move on, she asks her to sing and offers to learn her words.

subtype: Hiraeth for a home and language left behind [Actor]

In my first semester in Bengaluru, I kept my phone's keyboard switched to Urdu even though I had no one to type to in it. I'm Aparna, and yes, my family speaks Urdu at home in Lucknow; people are always surprised by that.
One night Zeenat, my lab partner, heard me talking to my mother and said, "Your voice changes completely when you speak it." She was right. In Kannada class I felt clumsy and slow. On the phone with Ammi I felt like myself.
I missed the old city lanes, the Muharram processions, the sound of our neighbour's radio through the wall. I told Zeenat our lane smelled of kebabs every evening. Later I remembered it also smelled of blocked drains. Distance had quietly cleaned up my memories, and I let it.

qa.q: Which city is Aparna's family home in?
qa.a: Aparna's family home is in Lucknow.

qa.q: Why did Aparna keep the keyboard in Urdu with no one to type to in it?
qa.a: Aparna was missing home and the language so much that seeing it on the screen gave comfort and a sense of being oneself in a city where Aparna felt clumsy and out of place.

qa.q: What could Aparna try so the longing feels less lonely in Bengaluru?
qa.a: Aparna could share the language and stories with people like Zeenat, or look for a group that speaks Urdu, so home becomes part of the new life instead of only an ache.

qa.a: Aparna might have kept the ache private; Zeenat's remark showed that someone saw how much the language meant to Aparna.

Hostel note, third week of October

Nazia, second-year chemistry, has been coming down to the common room most evenings to watch the local news channel from her home state with the sound very low. She does not seem to follow the stories; she listens to the voices.
Her roommate Zeenat mentioned that Nazia now cooks rice the way her mother does on a small kettle in the room and calls it "proper food". When I asked Nazia how she was, she said, "Fine, just missing Srinagar. Everything there was better." Then she added, smiling, "Even the traffic jams, apparently."
She is eating, attending classes and laughing with friends, so I am not worried about her safety. I told her about the students' language circle on Sundays and she said she might try it.

Saturday, before the trip: Zainab booked the overnight train to Bareilly and told her flatmate Uma, "I'm going to eat jalebis at Shafiq Chacha's stall and walk to the old tank and just sit."
Sunday, in the town: The stall was a mobile repair shop now. The tank had been filled in and a parking lot painted over it. Her school had a new gate and a name she didn't recognise. Zainab stood where the jalebi pan used to be and felt foolish for bringing an empty tiffin to fill.
Wednesday, back at work: Uma asked how it went. Zainab took a long time to answer. "The town is fine. It's just not the one I miss. I think I miss being fourteen there, with Abbu still coming home at six."
She kept the empty tiffin on her desk anyway.

qa.a: The stall was a mobile repair shop now.

"Salma puttar, sit. Your Dadaji will tell you. You ask why I never went back to live in Moga. I'll tell you.
When I was twenty-five, I, Amandeep, was working at a mill in Ludhiana. I saved leave for a whole year to go home for Lohri. I dreamed of our courtyard fire, my friends singing till late, my mother's makki roti.
I got off the bus and the fields near the road were houses. My friends had moved to Canada or to Delhi. The courtyard was cemented and the new tenants were kind but strangers. I stood by their fire for ten minutes and left.
On the bus back I cried like a child. Then I decided something: I would stop waiting for that Moga to return and light my own Lohri fire wherever I lived. Your Dadi and I did, every year."

qa.q: What festival did Amandeep save his leave to go home for?
qa.a: He saved leave for a whole year to go home for Lohri.

qa.q: What was young Amandeep feeling on the bus back from Moga?
qa.a: He was grieving and heartbroken, crying like a child, because the home he had longed for was gone and could not be brought back.

qa.q: What choice did Amandeep make on that bus ride, and why did it help?
qa.a: He decided to stop waiting for the old Moga to return and to light his own Lohri fire wherever he lived, which let him keep the feeling without chasing a vanished place.

qa.q: How might the new tenants have seen Amandeep standing by their fire?
qa.a: They were kind but likely puzzled, seeing only a stranger who stood quietly for ten minutes and left, not knowing what he had lost.

grounding: An elder recalls visiting his changed hometown as a young man and learning that his longing was for a time that could not be fully returned to.

subtype: Longing for a place that may no longer exist [Actor]
passage:
Suraj had only one afternoon in Darjeeling before the conference in Siliguri, and the fog came down just as his shared jeep arrived. He had planned the route for weeks: his old school, the bakery near the clock tower, the bend where you could see the mountain.
The school was locked for the holidays. The bakery had turned into a hotel lobby. The bend was just white cloud.
He texted Pema, his school friend who now lived in Pune: "Came home. Home isn't here."
Pema wrote back: "It never was a place, yaar. It was us at fifteen, with no bills. 🤍"
Suraj stood in the drizzle, oddly both warmed and emptied. The jeep driver honked twice. He bought a plain cake from a stall, because it smelled almost right, and climbed back in.

qa.q: What had the bakery near the clock tower become?
qa.a: The bakery had turned into a hotel lobby.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling as he stood in the drizzle after Pema's message?
qa.a: He felt oddly both warmed and emptied: comforted that Pema understood, but sad that the place and time he longed for could not come back.

qa.q: What would you advise Suraj to do with the rest of that short visit?
qa.a: He could accept the fog and closed doors, enjoy small things that still feel close, like the cake, and plan to share memories with Pema rather than chase old places.

qa.q: How is Pema affected by Suraj's message?
qa.a: Pema clearly shares the same longing and answers gently, turning Suraj's sad text into a shared memory of being fifteen together.

"Sabina, you asked why I call my mother every day at seven. Let me tell you something from when I was about your age.
I had moved to Chennai for my first job. When I went back to Madurai for Pongal, my room was exactly as I had left it, my old hair clips still on the shelf. I laughed at her. I said, 'Amma, rent it out.' She only said, 'It's your room, beti.'
That night I woke for water and saw her standing at my door, just looking at me sleeping. In the morning she was busy and cheerful again.
I, Leela, understood then that she had been waiting in that room for two years. After that, my calls were never short. Five minutes to me was the best part of her evening."

qa.a: She went home to Madurai for Pongal.

qa.a: Seeing Amma silently watching her sleep; it showed her that a short call meant a great deal, so she stopped keeping calls short.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt when Leela told her to rent out the room?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt and unseen, because the room was how she kept her daughter close while waiting.

grounding: An elder remembers noticing, as a young adult, her mother keeping her room unchanged and watching her sleep, and learning that love had become waiting.

The power was out across the whole block when Manoj reached home late on Friday, his flight delayed by rain. His friend Arnab had driven him from the airport and came up to help with the bag.
By the light of a phone torch they found the dining table set for one, the food covered with plates and gone cold. Manoj's father was asleep in the chair beside it, still in his shirt, an old album open on his lap at a photo of Manoj's first day at college.
Arnab whispered, "He waited for you."
Manoj stood very still. His father had said on the phone, "No need to hurry." He woke him gently. His father's first words were, "Eat something," and then, softer, "You're thin."
Manoj ate the cold food by torchlight and did not mention the delay.

The first winter in Toronto, I, Seema, lived on voice notes from Kolkata. I replayed Ma's messages on the bus so often I missed my stop twice. On weekends I stayed in and cried over old Durga Puja photos.
By spring I made a small rule for myself: home gets Sunday mornings, fully. I video call Ma, cook luchi, and listen to the old songs. The rest of the week belongs to here.
Ujjwal, a guy from my lab, invited me to a board-game night. I nearly said no. I went, and now I host it once a month and make aloo dum for everyone.
This October a few of us found a small community Puja in a school hall. I stood there with Ujjwal and felt Kolkata in my chest, warm, not sharp.

qa.a: Seema lived on voice notes from Kolkata.

qa.a: Giving home Sunday mornings fully and saying yes to game night; it kept the old rituals alive while also building friendships in the new city.

qa.a: Seema might have stayed alone with the old photos, and the longing would likely have kept pulling Seema out of life in Toronto.

When the bell rang, Tanvir walked beside Dhruv to the tap without talking. Finally he said, "I felt it too. Like it was me."

"Breathe," her friend Noa said, laughing.

Walking home, her voice was hoarse. "That felt like mine," she said. "Like we all won."
